title: Digital Asset Custody: A Complete Guide
summary: Digital asset custody is the secure management of cryptographic keys that authorize blockchain transactions. It includes governance, controls, and recovery processes to protect those assets.
body_markdown:
## Key Takeaways


-


Digital asset custody is the secure management of the private cryptographic keys that authorize blockchain transactions.


-


For institutions, custody decisions affect more than asset storage. They shape governance, regulatory compliance, and how digital assets move across the organization.


-


Evaluating a digital asset custodian requires looking beyond security to assess operational controls, insurance, asset segregation, audit standards, and regulatory status.


-


The right custody model should align with an institution's security requirements, governance framework, and long-term operational needs.


As regulated financial institutions enter digital assets, custody is one of the first and most important decisions they make. Before assets can be traded, staked, or held on behalf of clients, institutions need confidence that those assets can be secured, governed, and accessed through controls that support their operational and regulatory responsibilities.


Digital asset custody is the secure management of the private cryptographic keys that authorize blockchain transactions. Unlike traditional financial custody, where custodians safeguard securities while ownership records remain within established financial systems, digital asset custody centers on controlling the cryptographic keys that authorize movement of the assets. If those keys are lost or compromised, the associated assets may be permanently inaccessible.


As a result, institutions evaluate custody differently than they would in traditional markets. Security remains fundamental alongside governance, operational controls, and regulatory oversight. The custody decision shapes how digital assets can be governed, moved, and used across the institution.


## Custody Models: Self-Custody, Third-Party, and Hybrid


No single custody model fits every institution. The right approach depends on an organization's regulatory obligations, operating model, risk tolerance, and how it plans to use digital assets. The difference is who controls the keys and who is responsible for protecting them.


With self-custody, the institution controls its own private keys and assumes responsibility for security, governance, recovery, and day-to-day operations. This approach offers the greatest control and flexibility but also places the full operational burden on the organization.


With third-party custody, those responsibilities shift to a digital asset custodian. The custodian secures the keys while providing operational controls such as approval workflows, audit trails, reporting, and recovery procedures. For many institutions, this reduces operational complexity and supports existing governance and compliance requirements.


A hybrid custody model combines elements of both approaches. Institutions may retain control over certain approvals or key shares while relying on a custodian for secure infrastructure, policy enforcement, and operational support. This balances direct control with institutional-grade security and oversight.


Many institutions use more than one custody model. For example, long-term treasury assets may remain with a qualified custodian while self-custody or hybrid arrangements support specialized operational needs. The right choice depends on the institution's governance, regulatory obligations, and operational needs.

## What Qualified Custodial Cold Storage Actually Means Operationally


For institutions, the value of[cold storage](https://www.bitgo.com/products/cold-wallets/?utm_source=blog&utm_medium=custody&utm_campaign=digital_asset_custody_guide&utm_source=blog&utm_medium=foundational&utm_campaign=digital_asset_custody_guide) lies less in keeping keys offline than in how the environment is operated. Qualified custodial cold storage shifts much of the operational responsibility from the institution to the custodian.


With qualified custodial cold storage, institutions do not manage hardware devices or backup copies of private keys. The custodian protects the underlying key material using physical, technical, and procedural controls designed to reduce the risk of unauthorized access or a single point of failure.


That operating model changes how assets move. Instead of signing transactions directly, institutions submit withdrawal requests through established workflows. The custodian verifies identities, enforces transaction policies, and completes the required approval process before authorizing a transfer. While this may add modest processing time compared to[self-managed wallets](https://www.bitgo.com/products/self-custody/?utm_source=blog&utm_medium=custody&utm_campaign=digital_asset_custody_guide&utm_source=blog&utm_medium=foundational&utm_campaign=digital_asset_custody_guide) , it also reduces the institution's operational burden.


Those workflows enforce governance controls. Segregation of duties helps ensure no single individual can initiate and approve a transaction. Policy controls can require multiple approvals, apply transaction limits, restrict transfers to approved destinations, and generate audit trails that support compliance and internal oversight.


Insurance is part of that operating model. Coverage is generally tied to the custodian's insurance program and the controls supporting that environment. Self-managed cold wallets may provide strong security, but they typically do not benefit from the same institutional insurance arrangements.


During due diligence, institutions should ask where key material is secured, how withdrawals are authorized, who can approve transactions, and what controls govern asset movement.


## Evaluating Key Management Architecture: What Institutions Should Ask


Multisignature (multisig) and[multi-party computation](https://www.bitgo.com/resources/blog/mpc-crypto-wallets-multi-party-computation-security/?utm_source=blog&utm_medium=brand&utm_campaign=digital_asset_custody_guide&utm_source=blog&utm_medium=foundational&utm_campaign=digital_asset_custody_guide) (MPC) often dominate discussions about digital asset custody. For institutions, however, the more important question is how the architecture supports accountability, governance, and long-term operational resilience.


Transaction authorization is the starting point. Every asset movement should produce a clear record showing who approved the transaction, what policies were applied, and whether the required approval process was followed. Institutions need evidence that governance controls are consistently enforced, not simply that a transaction was successfully signed.


Recovery planning is just as important. Institutions should understand what happens if a signing key or key share is lost, compromised, or becomes unavailable. Recovery procedures should be documented, regularly tested, and designed to restore access without creating new security or operational risks.


Institutions should also evaluate whether the custody architecture is portable. If business requirements change, can assets be moved to another custodian without unnecessary complexity? Understanding the migration process helps avoid operational lock-in.


Custody platforms also need to evolve. Cryptographic standards change, and custody platforms require periodic upgrades. Custodians should be able to explain how new protocols are independently audited, tested, and deployed while maintaining governance controls and protecting client assets.


## Qualified Custody: What It Means and Why It Matters


Under the SEC's[Custody Rule](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/17/275.206%284%29-2) , investment advisers with custody of client funds or securities are generally required to maintain those assets with a qualified custodian. While the regulatory framework for digital assets continues to evolve, not every digital asset custodian meets those standards. Institutions should consult legal counsel when evaluating their specific regulatory obligations.


The rescission of Staff Accounting Bulletin (SAB) 121 through SAB 122 removed SEC staff[accounting guidance](https://dart.deloitte.com/USDART/home/publications/deloitte/heads-up/2025/sec-rescinds-sab-121-issues-sab-122-crypto-cryptocurrency) that had required certain entities safeguarding crypto assets for platform users to recognize a safeguarding obligation on their balance sheets. As more regulated financial institutions evaluate digital asset custody, institutions should verify a provider's regulatory status rather than assume it.


The SEC's September 2025[no-action letter](https://www.sec.gov/rules-regulations/no-action-interpretive-exemptive-letters/division-investment-management-staff-no-action-interpretive-letters/simpsonthacherbartlett093025) stated that staff would not recommend enforcement action if registered advisers and regulated funds treat certain state trust companies as “banks” for purposes of the applicable custody provisions, subject to the conditions described in the letter. Verify which legal entity is acting as the custodian and what regulatory framework governs that entity.


During due diligence, institutions should verify the custodian's regulatory license, operating jurisdictions, whether it serves as the primary custodian or relies on a sub-custodian, and how client assets are legally segregated. Qualified custodian status is not self-certified and should always be independently verified.

## Insurance, Segregation, and Audit Standards


Every custodian claims strong insurance coverage, asset segregation, and independent audits. During due diligence, institutions should understand how these protections work and where their limits begin.


Insurance coverage varies significantly between custodians. Ask who underwrites the policy, whether it applies to cold storage, and whether the limits are appropriate for the assets being held. Institutions should also understand what is excluded, since user error, phishing attacks, protocol failures, and certain forms of insider misconduct may not be covered.


Asset segregation policies should be reviewed just as carefully. Institutions should determine whether client assets are held in individually designated accounts or pooled with other client holdings, and whether that segregation is supported by the custodian's legal structure. Legal segregation can provide stronger protection if the custodian experiences financial distress.


Independent audits provide another layer of verification.[SOC 2 Type II](https://www.ispartnersllc.com/blog/understand-the-difference-soc-1-type-1-2-reports/) reports demonstrate that operational controls have been evaluated over a defined period, while[proof of reserves](https://www.thenetworkfirm.com/blog/proof-of-reserves-vs-financial-statement-audits-what-crypto-companies-need-to-know) can help verify reported holdings against client obligations at a point in time. Institutions should ask how frequently these assessments are performed, whether they are independently attested, and whether detailed reports are available during due diligence.


## Evaluating Digital Asset Custody Providers in 2026


Institutions once evaluated custody providers primarily on security and asset support. Those capabilities still matter, but they no longer tell the whole story. As regulated financial institutions expand their digital asset activities, custody has become an operational and regulatory decision as much as a security decision.


Rather than evaluating individual product features, institutions should assess how the custody platform functions as part of their broader operating model. Regulatory status, key management, cold storage controls, governance, asset segregation, and audit standards should work together as a single control framework rather than independent capabilities.


Custody platforms should also be evaluated in the context of the broader business. Institutions need to understand whether the platform can support additional digital asset activities as their business evolves. Asset coverage, geographic licensing, policy controls, reporting, treasury integration, and operational workflows all affect whether a custody platform can scale alongside the organization.


Institutions are selecting long-term infrastructure, not simply a security product. The strongest providers combine secure custody with the governance, operational maturity, and regulatory foundation needed to support institutional participation as digital asset markets continue to develop.

## FAQs


### What is digital asset custody?


Digital asset custody is the secure management of the private cryptographic keys that authorize blockchain transactions. It also includes the governance, operational controls, and recovery processes needed to protect those assets over time.


### What is the difference between self-custody and institutional crypto custody?


With self-custody, the asset owner manages and secures their own private keys. Institutional crypto custody shifts much of that operational responsibility to a specialized custodian that provides security infrastructure, governance controls, audit trails, and compliance support. Some organizations also use hybrid custody models that combine elements of both approaches.


### What is a qualified custodian for digital assets?


A qualified custodian is a regulated financial institution that meets applicable legal and regulatory requirements for safeguarding client assets. Institutions should consult legal counsel regarding applicable custody requirements and independently verify a custodian's regulatory status.


### How is digital asset custody different from traditional custody?


Traditional custodians safeguard securities, while digital asset custodians secure the private cryptographic keys that control blockchain assets. Because blockchain transactions are generally irreversible, protecting those keys becomes a central part of the custody function.


### What should institutions evaluate when comparing crypto custody providers?


Institutions should evaluate a provider's regulatory status, key management architecture, cold storage operations, governance controls, legal asset segregation, insurance coverage, audit standards, supported assets, geographic licensing, operational track record, and withdrawal procedures.
